---
title: "Creating elements"
---

Every element you have changed so far was already sitting in `index.html`. You
looked it up and wrote into it. Most real pages are not like that. A to-do list
starts empty and grows while the user types. A web shop shows one row per
article in the cart, and nobody wrote those rows by hand. The page comes from
data, and your program builds it.

## Three names, three list items {#sec-creating-elements-experiment}

Make a fresh app from the starter and open `index.html`. Change the heading and
put an empty list under it:

```html
<h1 id="helloWorldHeader">Names</h1>
<ul id="nameList"></ul>
```

Now replace everything in `src/index.ts` with this:

```ts
const names = ['Ada', 'Grace', 'Linus'];

const list = document.querySelector<HTMLUListElement>('#nameList');
if (!list) {
  throw new Error('No element with the id nameList');
}

for (const name of names) {
  const item = document.createElement('li');
  item.textContent = name;
  list.append(item);
}
```

Run `npm start`. Three list items appear under the heading, one per name, even
though the `<ul>` in your HTML is empty. Add a fourth name to the array and
save. The page reloads and shows four.

## Data in, elements out {#sec-creating-elements-pattern}

That loop is the pattern this book comes back to in almost every project.
You have data in a variable, and you want the user to see it, so you walk over
the data and build one element per entry.

Three steps make one element:

1. `document.createElement('li')` builds a new element object of that tag.
2. `item.textContent = name` fills it, exactly like the elements you already
   know.
3. `list.append(item)` puts it into the page.

Step 2 uses `textContent` on purpose. The to-do list below puts text that a
user typed into an element, and `textContent` writes those characters onto the
page as characters. Type `<b>hi</b>` and the page shows the angle brackets.
`innerHTML` would read the same characters as markup and build a bold element
out of them, which hands anyone who types into your page a way to put their own
HTML into it. Text from a user goes in through `textContent`.

Step 3 is the one people forget. `createElement` gives you a real object with
all the properties you know, but that object has no parent yet, so it is
nowhere on the page. You can set its text and change its style, and the user
still sees nothing. An element becomes visible the moment you attach it to an
element that is already in the tree.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Nothing appears, no error

If your new elements never show up, the missing `append` is the first thing to
check. The browser reports no error for it. From its point of view you built an
object and then never used it.
:::

`append` puts the new element after the parent's existing children.
`prepend` puts it in front of them, so the newest entry sits at the top of the
list. And `item.remove()` takes an element out of the tree again. You call it
on the element itself, and it disappears from the page together with everything
inside it.

## A stylesheet of your own {#sec-creating-elements-styles}

Setting `item.style.color` on every single element gets tiring fast, and it
mixes the look of the page into the logic of your program. CSS does that job
better. You have copied a stylesheet into an app before; this time you write
one. Create the file `src/styles.css`:

```css
li:hover {
  background-color: #eee;
}

li.done {
  text-decoration: line-through;
  color: gray;
}
```

Then make the very first line of `src/index.ts` the import that pulls it in:

```ts
import './styles.css';
```

Vite sees the import and puts the styles into the page for you. Every project
from here on has a `src/styles.css` reaching the page this way.

Each block in the file has a **selector** in front of the braces, which says
which elements the rules apply to. `li:hover` means any `li` while the mouse
pointer is over it. `li.done` means any `li` that carries the label `done`. Try
the hover rule right now: reload the page and move the mouse over the names. A
later chapter takes the selector language apart properly.

## Labels on elements {#sec-creating-elements-classlist}

A **class** in HTML is a label you stick on an element so CSS can find it. An
element can carry several of them, and every element has a `classList`
property to manage them. Add a click handler to the loop in your experiment:

```ts
for (const name of names) {
  const item = document.createElement('li');
  item.textContent = name;
  item.addEventListener('click', () => {
    item.classList.add('done');
  });
  list.append(item);
}
```

Click a name. It turns gray and gets a line through it, because
`classList.add('done')` put the label on the element and the `li.done` rule in
your stylesheet was waiting for exactly that. `classList.remove('done')` peels
the label off again.

This is a better habit than reaching for `item.style` every time. The
stylesheet decides how "done" looks, your program decides which items are
done, and you can restyle the whole app without touching a line of TypeScript.

::: {.callout-note}
## Two meanings of one word

The word `class` in HTML and CSS has nothing to do with the `class` keyword in
TypeScript, which arrives in a later part of this book. Same word, two
completely different things. When this chapter says class, it means the label.
:::

::: {.research title="What else can classList do?"}
`add` and `remove` are two of several `classList` methods, and the to-do list
below needs two more. MDN documents all of them on one page, the reference
page for the `classList` property of an element.

1. Which `classList` method switches a class on when it is off and off when it
   is on, in a single call?
2. Which `classList` method answers `true` or `false` for the question "does
   this element already carry that class?"
3. `append` and `appendChild` both put an element into a parent. Name one thing
   `append` accepts that `appendChild` refuses.

For the exam you need to switch a class on and off and ask whether it is set,
without looking either up.
:::

## Exercise: a to-do list {#sec-creating-elements-exercise}

{{< exercise todo-list >}}

The `index.html` you copied has a text input with the id `todoText`, a button
with the id `addTodo`, an empty `<ul id="todos">`, and an empty paragraph
`<p id="openCount">` under the list. The stylesheet already styles
`#todos li.done` and highlights an item on hover.

1. Add `import './styles.css';` as the first line of `src/index.ts`, then look
   up the input, the button, the list, and the paragraph with
   `querySelector<T>`. Throw an error if one of them is missing. Run
   `npm start`. The page shows the heading, the input, and the button, and
   nothing happens yet.
2. Listen for a click on the button. Read `input.value`, build an `li` with
   that text, and append it to the list. Empty text is ignored, so check for it
   and stop early. After adding, set `input.value` back to an empty string so
   the field is ready for the next item. Type something, click **Add**, and the
   item appears in the list.
   *Tip:* `input.value.trim()` gives you the text without spaces at the start
   and the end, so a field with only spaces counts as empty.
3. Give every new `li` a click handler that flips the class `done` on it. One
   click crosses the item out, the next click brings it back. The research task
   above tells you which `classList` method does both directions in one call.
4. Inside every new `li`, add a small button with the text `x` and give that
   button its own click handler. When it is clicked, remove the whole item with
   `remove()`. Watch out for one thing: the handler must remove the `li`, not
   the button, so create the `li` first, keep it in a variable, and use that
   variable inside the button's handler.
5. Test all three actions together: add four items, cross two of them out, and
   delete one of the crossed-out ones. The rest of the list stays as it was.

**Bonus.** Fill the paragraph `#openCount` with a line like `3 open` and update
it after every add, every toggle, and every delete. To count, walk over
`list.children`, which is the collection of the elements currently inside the
list, and count the ones that do *not* carry the class `done`. The research
task above tells you which `classList` method answers that. Writing the
counting code in its own function pays off here, because you call it from three
places.
